concepts.title: What Are Rights? Claims Backed by Society and Law

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'What Are Rights? Claims Backed by Society and Law' refers to.
questions.a: A right is a claim that a person is entitled to make on society -- to speak, to practise a faith, to move freely -- which the community and its laws recognise and are bound to respect. Rights supply what one cannot secure alone: a social guarantee that one's vital interests will be honoured.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'What Are Rights? Claims Backed by Society and Law'.
questions.a: Rights are entitlements, not favours -- claims others are obliged to honour.

questions.q: Under which section is 'What Are Rights? Claims Backed by Society and Law' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: keps105.txt lines 1-90 (introduction, definition of rights as claims, rights as necessary conditions for a dignified life))

concepts.title: Where Rights Come From: Natural, Historical and Legal Bases

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Where Rights Come From: Natural, Historical and Legal Bases' refers to.
questions.a: Thinkers ground rights differently: as natural rights inhering in human beings before any state; as historical gains won through long struggles, from Magna Carta to freedom movements; or as legal rights created and listed by constitutions. Most modern theorists blend these -- rights are human claims given shape by history and guaranteed by law.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Where Rights Come From: Natural, Historical and Legal Bases'.
questions.a: Born as moral claims, hardened by struggle, sealed by law -- rights carry all three ancestries.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Where Rights Come From: Natural, Historical and Legal Bases' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: keps105.txt lines 90-170 (natural rights, historical evolution of rights, legal rights and constitutional guarantees))

concepts.title: Rights and Duties: The Two Sides of One Claim

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Rights and Duties: The Two Sides of One Claim' refers to.
questions.a: Every right implies duties: my freedom of speech obliges others to tolerate my expression, while my rights survive only inside a society where I too perform my obligations -- respecting others' identical rights, obeying just laws, contributing to common resources.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Rights and Duties: The Two Sides of One Claim'.
questions.a: A right on one side is a duty on the other -- claim and obligation are one relation seen twice.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Rights and Duties: The Two Sides of One Claim' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: keps105.txt lines 170-240 (rights and duties, why duties accompany rights, mutual respect among right holders))

concepts.title: Rights in a Democracy and Their Political Importance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Rights in a Democracy and Their Political Importance' refers to.
questions.a: Rights make democracy real for each person: they protect dissent between elections, secure the free information votes depend on, and shield minorities from majority whims. A democracy without enforceable rights can be majoritarian pressure dressed as rule by the people.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Rights in a Democracy and Their Political Importance'.
questions.a: Elections choose rulers; rights keep them civilised between elections.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Rights in a Democracy and Their Political Importance' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.4 (source: keps105.txt lines 240-320 (rights in a democracy, why rights are needed for democratic participation, protection of minorities and dissent))

concepts.title: Rights of the Accused, and the Right to Resist

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Rights of the Accused, and the Right to Resist' refers to.
questions.a: Rights extend even to those suspected of crimes: fair trial, legal defence and protection from torture mark a civilised system, for guilt must be proved, not presumed. And when a state turns systematically tyrannical, political theory recognises a residual right to resist -- the warrant behind struggles against colonial and dictatorial rule.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Rights of the Accused, and the Right to Resist'.
questions.a: Justice is measured at its margins -- by the rights of the accused and by when resistance becomes legitimate.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Rights of the Accused, and the Right to Resist' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.5 (source: keps105.txt lines 320-400 (rights of accused and arrested persons, right against torture, right to constitutional remedies, right to resist tyranny))
